newsitem.title: USA: MSRB staff to raise adequacy of consultants rule.
newsitem.headline: MSRB staff to raise adequacy of consultants rule.

text.p: Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board is expected to take up the adequacy of its pay-to-play rule for consultants later this month following a a new press report of millions of dollars of questionable consulting fees in New Jersey, a board official said.

"The board will be (made) aware" of the article, Christopher Taylor, MSRB executive director Christopher Taylor said in a telephone interview. "This information will clearly be in front of the board at its next meeting now scheduled" for the end of the month, Taylor added.
MSRB's rule G-38 requires muni dealers to disclose information quarterly to the public about their arrangements with the consultants they hire to help them win bond business.

The Bergen Record of Bergen County, N.J. reported on April 13 that seven securities firms last year paid 10 consultants a total of $845,000 to help them win a share of the millions of dollars in underwriting fees generated by state and local bond issues in New Jersey each year.

The Record, which surveyed disclosure forms that bond firms filed with the MSRB's annex in Alexandria, Va., said the seven firms handled at least 40 percent of the negotiated bonds issued by New Jersey last year. The seven firms comprise only two percent of all bond firms registered with the board nationwide, the paper said.

Taylor said the board at present has no plans to revise either rule G-38 or its predecessor, three-year-old rule G-37, which bars muni dealers that make contributions to issuer clients from doing business for two years with those governments. But he said the Bergen Record article will be on the table at the board's three-day meeting between April 30 to May 2 in Washington, D.C.

Taylor stressed that no one press article can serve as the basis for MSRB action. But added that the Bergen Record article may demonstrate how data from the board's repository can be used to mirror possible industry practices.
Taylor added: "The board is constantly monitoring industry practice and has stated in many cases that it will be watching what is happening in all areas."
